title: Inheritance and Verdict
premise: Estate lawyer Quentin Winterbourne is retained by a dying client, Marguerite Ashcombe, to read a will that names her as already murdered — and pays him to prove the murder hasn't happened yet. Following a ledger concealed in the will's marginalia, Quentin uncovers a family fortune built on a decades-old wrongful verdict, with three Ashcombe heirs each holding a motive to make the prophecy true. As Marguerite's health fails on schedule, Quentin realizes the 'future murder' is a trap she designed to force the family's crimes into the open: the killer she predicts is the one who silenced the original witness. In the end, Quentin chooses justice outside the law, exposing the verdict's corruption publicly while letting the family destroy itself — and inherits, unexpectedly, the burden of Marguerite's own confession.
about_author: Felix Underhill is the pen name of a former probate clerk who spent eleven years in the back rooms of county courthouses before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about paperwork, power, and the people who fall between the lines.

chapters.title: The Will That Reads Backwards
chapters.summary: Quentin Winterbourne, jaded estate lawyer, is summoned to Ashcombe Hall to read the will of Marguerite Ashcombe — a will that opens by declaring her own future murder and naming Quentin as investigator. Third-person limited POV. The emotional beat is cold professional curiosity curdling into unease as Quentin realizes the document is dated three days in the future.

chapters.title: Payment in Advance
chapters.summary: Marguerite, frail and lucid, explains the retainer: prove her murder hasn't happened — yet — and the fee is already in his trust account. Quentin's POV. He wants to refuse; the money and her certainty hook him. The beat is reluctant complicity, a man signing a contract with something he can't name.

chapters.title: Three Heirs, One House
chapters.summary: Quentin meets the heirs: eldest son Edmund, who manages the estate; daughter Vivian, a judge's wife with sharp eyes; and the youngest, Casper, recently returned from abroad. Quentin's POV. Everyone performs grief in advance. The beat is a house full of people rehearsing for a funeral no one will admit to expecting.

chapters.title: Marginalia
chapters.summary: Studying the will overnight, Quentin notices numbers and names woven into its clause numbering — a ledger hidden in plain sight. Quentin's POV. The beat is the thrill of the puzzle colliding with dread: the ledger tracks payments made after a 1979 criminal verdict that sent a gardener, Thomas Reeve, to prison for a death the Ashcombes caused.

chapters.title: The Gardener's Verdict
chapters.summary: Quentin digs into court archives and finds Reeve convicted of manslaughter in the death of a housekeeper, Lorna Pell — a verdict secured by the Ashcombe family's lawyers. Quentin's POV. The beat is dawning outrage: the ledger's payments look like hush money to someone who knew the truth.

chapters.title: A Witness Who Won't Die
chapters.summary: Quentin tracks down the ledger's payee — an elderly woman, Ruth Pell, Lorna's sister, who has received monthly sums for forty years. Ruth's POV, her first. She reveals she saw what really happened and was paid for silence, but the payments stopped last month. The beat is terror: the family is closing the account — and the witness — permanently.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Knew
chapters.summary: Quentin confronts Marguerite; she admits Lorna's death was no accident and that she was the one who hired the lawyers who buried it. Marguerite's POV via a dictated confession scene. The beat is corrosive guilt: her 'predicted murder' is a mechanism she built to force the truth out before she dies.

chapters.title: The Stopped Payments
chapters.summary: Quentin learns Edmund cut Ruth's payments after finding the ledger — meaning Edmund knows a witness exists. Quentin's POV. The beat is acceleration: the murder Marguerite predicted now has a likely perpetrator, a method, and a deadline.

chapters.title: Vivian's Verdict
chapters.summary: Quentin approaches Vivian, whose husband is the judge whose father presided over Reeve's trial. Vivian's POV. She knows more than she admits and offers Quentin a bribe to drop the matter — then warns him that Casper isn't what he seems. The beat is corrupted power extending a polite hand.

chapters.title: The Man Named Casper
chapters.summary: Quentin discovers 'Casper' is not an Ashcombe at all: he is Thomas Reeve's grandson, inserted into the family under a false identity, hunting the same truth. Casper's POV, his first. The beat is two investigators recognizing each other — allies, or rivals for the same revenge.

chapters.title: Ledger, Completed
chapters.summary: Casper and Quentin pool findings: the ledger's final entries, in Marguerite's hand, schedule her own death and name the instrument — her heart medication, already swapped. Quentin's POV. The beat is horrified clarity: Marguerite has scripted her murder to frame whoever acts, and someone has taken the bait.

chapters.title: Deadline at the Hall
chapters.summary: With Marguerite's health collapsing on schedule, Quentin tries to swap the medication back, but the pills have vanished from his evidence bag — someone in the house is watching him. Quentin's POV. The beat is paranoia: the invisible investigator has become the visible suspect.

chapters.title: The Inquest of One
chapters.summary: Quentin is detained after a break-in at Marguerite's rooms; Edmund produces evidence framing him. Interrogation scene, Quentin's POV, told with lawyerly precision. The beat is the machinery of law — the very system that failed Reeve — now grinding toward Quentin himself.

chapters.title: Ruth's Testimony
chapters.summary: Released on a technicality, Quentin races to Ruth Pell, who has decided to finally speak. Ruth's POV. She gives him her forty years of records — and reveals one detail the ledger never showed: Marguerite was present the night Lorna died. The beat is the ground shifting under every alliance.

chapters.title: Confession, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Quentin returns to the Hall to force a full confession from Marguerite on record; he finds her mid-stroke, and Edmund blocking the doctor's call. Quentin's POV. The beat is helpless fury — the murder happening in slow motion, exactly as the will foretold, with the whole family as audience.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Second Will
chapters.summary: Marguerite survives just long enough for Quentin to read her second will: it disinherits everyone unless her murderer is named within seven days, and grants Quentin authority to convene a private inquest. Quentin's POV. The beat is the trap snapping shut — on the family, and on him.

chapters.title: Seven Days
chapters.summary: The heirs circle: Edmund offers Quentin a partnership, Vivian threatens disbarment, Casper pushes for exposure at any cost. Rotating close POVs across the household. The beat is a siege in silk, each character revealing what inheritance means to them — money, impunity, or justice.

chapters.title: The Swapped Vial
chapters.summary: Quentin reconstructs the medication swap and finds the proof: Vivian took the pills, believing Marguerite's death would protect her husband's judicial legacy — not knowing Marguerite had already documented the swap. Vivian's POV. The beat is the corrupt inheriting the corruption they were born into.

chapters.title: Inquest at Ashcombe Hall
chapters.summary: Quentin convenes the private inquest in the great hall, presenting the ledger, Ruth's testimony, and Marguerite's recordings — laying the 1979 verdict and Vivian's act side by side. Quentin's POV. The beat is catharsis through procedure: the law failing, then a rougher justice prevailing in the same room.

chapters.title: Verdicts
chapters.summary: Vivian confesses to the swap; Edmund's financial crimes surface; Casper publicly clears his grandfather's name. The police take over what Quentin began. Multiple POVs converging. The beat is the cost of justice: no one leaves the hall whole, but no one leaves it lying.

chapters.title: The Estate of Quentin Winterbourne
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Quentin executes the final bequest: Marguerite's fortune funds a foundation in Lorna and Thomas Reeve's names, and her confession is published. Quentin's POV, quiet and reflective. The beat is inheritance redefined — not what you're given, but what you agree to carry.

chapters.title: A New Client
chapters.summary: Closing scene: a stranger arrives at Quentin's office with a will dated three days in the future, asking him to prove a murder that hasn't happened yet. Quentin's POV. The beat is an ambiguous, chilling coda — Marguerite's method has escaped into the world, and Quentin must decide whether to open the door.
